questions.explanation: To understand thermal stability, we look at how the DNA strands are held together. In the DNA double helix, bases pair up via hydrogen bonds. A fundamental difference exists in the strength of these pairs: - G-C pairs form 3 hydrogen bonds . - A-T pairs form 2 hydrogen bonds . Since E. coli is more G-C rich than yeast, its DNA contains a higher density of these triple-bonded pairs. Thermal stability refers to how much heat energy is needed to 'denature' or pull the two DNA strands apart. Because each G-C pair has an extra hydrogen bond compared to an A-T pair, more thermal energy is required to break the collective attractive forces holding the strands together. Because the E. coli genome has a higher percentage of G-C base pairs, it possesses greater thermal stability. questions.explanation: To answer this, we first need to understand that electron microscopes offer much higher resolution than light microscopes. Resolution is the ability to distinguish between two separate points. While light microscopes are limited by the wavelength of visible light to a resolution of about 200 nm, electron microscopes use electron beams with much shorter wavelengths, achieving resolutions as high as 0.2 nm. This is 1,000 times better than a light microscope! Because of this superior resolution, scientists can see the ultrastructure of the cell—the detailed internal anatomy that is invisible under a light microscope. Before electron microscopy, many organelles appeared as mere dots or were completely invisible. The electron microscope led to the discovery and detailed study of specific organelles. questions.explanation: To explain intracellular digestion, we first identify the organelle responsible. Lysosomes are spherical organelles that contain hydrolytic enzymes . This relates to Topic B2.2 Organelles and compartmentalization , where the function of lysosomes is detailed. These hydrolytic enzymes function by breaking down large macromolecules (proteins, lipids, nucleic acids, and carbohydrates) into their smaller components through hydrolysis reactions. The cell maintains itself by digesting its own damaged or old organelles (such as non-functional mitochondria). This specific process of self-digestion is known as autophagy . In addition to internal maintenance, these enzymes are used to break down external threats, such as pathogens (bacteria and viruses) that the cell has engulfed. This collective breakdown of materials inside the cell boundary is referred to as intracellular digestion . The breakdown products (like amino acids and simple sugars) are not wasted. They are released into the cytoplasm and recycled as building blocks to synthesize new molecules and structures needed by the cell. questions.question_text: Outline how the presence of a cell wall contributes to maintaining cell shape and function.
questions.correct_answer: Cell wall provides structural support/protection to cell; Maintains cell shape/prevents cell from bursting; Prevents excessive water uptake into cell; Resists turgor pressure/prevents excessive expansion/bursting of the cell; <note> Award marks for clearly explained points about cell wall function. Accept other valid points related to structural integrity and osmotic regulation.</note>
questions.explanation: To answer this question, we focus on the cell wall , which is the rigid outer layer found in plant cells, bacteria, and fungi. This concept relates to Topic A2.2 Cell structure and the mechanics of water movement in Topic D2.3 Water potential . The question asks for an outline, so we need to briefly explain the mechanism behind its functions rather than just listing them. The first major contribution of the cell wall is providing mechanical strength and structural support . Unlike the flexible plasma membrane, the cell wall is rigid (often made of cellulose in plants). This rigidity defines and maintains the cell's specific shape , protecting the interior organelles and allowing the organism to grow upright against gravity. Cells often exist in environments where water naturally enters them via osmosis. As water flows in, the volume of the cytoplasm increases, exerting an outward pressure on the cell membrane known as turgor pressure . The cell wall contributes to function by resisting this turgor pressure . It provides a counter-force that limits further expansion. This turgidity is actually beneficial, as it makes plant tissues stiff and able to support leaves and flowers. Finall

questions.question_text: Explain how the presence of a central vacuole contributes to maintaining cell shape and function.
questions.correct_answer: Central vacuole stores water/cell sap which creates turgor pressure; Turgor pressure is the pressure exerted by cell contents against the cell wall; This pressure pushes against the rigid cell wall; The pressure maintains cell rigidity/turgidity and overall cell shape; <note>Award marks for clearly linked steps showing understanding of how vacuole function leads to cell shape maintenance. Accept reference to nutrients/waste storage but ensure connection to turgor pressure is made.</note>
questions.explanation: First, we look at the primary content of the central vacuole. The central vacuole stores water and dissolved substances (often called cell sap). Water moves into the vacuole (usually by osmosis) because the solute concentration inside is higher than in the cytoplasm or outside the cell. As water accumulates inside the vacuole, it swells and takes up more space. This accumulation generates a specific type of hydrostatic pressure known as turgor pressure . This is a key concept in plant biology covered in Topic D2.3: Water potential . The expanding vacuole pushes the cytoplasm and plasma membrane outwards. This turgor pressure exerts a physical force directly against the rigid cell wall surrounding the plant cell. The cell wall is strong and resists this outward pressure. This balance of forces makes the cell firm, or turgid . This turgidity is what maintains the fixed shape of the cell and provides structural support to the plant, allowing it to stand upright.

questions.question_text: Explain how reverse transcriptase allows retroviruses to replicate within a host cell.

questions.explanation: To understand how retroviruses (like HIV) function, we must first identify their unique tool: reverse transcriptase . Normally, cells follow the "Central Dogma" of biology, where DNA is transcribed into RNA. However, retroviruses carry their genetic information as RNA . To replicate, they use reverse transcriptase, an enzyme they produce and carry within their viral capsid, to reverse this normal flow of information. The process begins when the retrovirus attaches to and enters a specific host cell (such as a T-lymphocyte). Once the virus has successfully entered the cytoplasm, it releases its viral RNA and the reverse transcriptase enzyme into the host's internal environment. In the cytoplasm, reverse transcriptase performs its primary job: it converts (transcribes) the viral RNA into a single strand of DNA . This is a critical step because the host cell's machinery is designed to read DNA, not viral RNA, to make proteins. The enzyme doesn't stop at a single strand. It uses the first DNA strand as a template to synthesize a complementary strand, resulting in a double-stranded DNA version of the viral genome. questions.explanation: The question asks us to outline the impact of viruses on global health for 4 marks. Using a thematic categorization approach, we will group the effects into three main areas: biological/health, economic, and systemic/infrastructure. This ensures we cover all the necessary points from the markscheme systematically. At the most fundamental level, viruses affect the physical well-being of populations. * Morbidity and Mortality: Viruses cause widespread illness ( morbidity ) and death ( mortality ). questions.explanation: This question asks for the replication process of a lytic virus. We will explain this using the Chronological Stages approach, which breaks the life cycle down into five sequential steps: Attachment , Penetration , Biosynthesis , Assembly , and Lysis . This relates to Topic A2.3 Viruses , specifically the lytic cycle. The first stage is attachment (or adsorption). The virus finds a suitable host cell and binds to its surface. Crucially, the virus must attach to specific receptors on the host's cell membrane, functioning like a lock and key. This specificity determines which cells a virus can infect. Once attached, the virus proceeds to penetration (or entry). The virus injects its genetic material (DNA or RNA) into the cytoplasm of the host cell, leaving the protein coat (capsid) outside in the case of bacteriophages, or entering entirely for some animal viruses. During biosynthesis (replication and synthesis), the virus takes control of the host cell. It uses the host's machinery (like enzymes, ribosomes, and ATP) to replicate its own genetic material and synthesize viral proteins. Key actions here: 1. questions.explanation: This question addresses how the field of taxonomy has evolved. It relates directly to Topic A3.2 Classification and cladistics (HL) , specifically focusing on how evidence from A3.2.6 Base sequences helps taxonomists verify evolutionary relationships that were previously guessed based on physical appearance. To answer this, we must first compare the fundamental data sources used in each era. Traditional Classification: relied on observing morphological (physical) characteristics . Taxonomists grouped organisms based on visible similarities, such as the shape of limbs, presence of wings, or bone structure. Modern Classification: utilizes molecular techniques , such as DNA sequencing. This allows scientists to analyze the base sequences of genes or amino acid sequences of proteins, providing a much more detailed and quantifiable dataset. Why was a change needed? The comparative approach highlights a critical flaw in relying solely on morphology. Organisms that are not closely related can evolve similar physical traits if they live in similar environments or face similar selective pressures. This is known as convergent evolution . questions.question_text: Explain how molecular evidence has supported the theory of evolution.
questions.correct_answer: DNA/protein sequences show similarities between species; These molecular similarities indicate common ancestry; Phylogenetic trees can be constructed using molecular data; These trees show evolutionary relationships between species; Trees indicate when species diverged from common ancestors; Greater molecular differences generally indicate longer time since divergence; Molecular evidence can determine relative rates of evolution; Molecular data supports morphological/fossil evidence for evolution; <note>Award marks for other relevant molecular evidence that supports evolution</note>
questions.explanation: The question asks us to explain how molecular evidence supports the theory of evolution. This specifically relates to Topic A4.1: Evolution and speciation and Topic A3.2: Classification and cladistics . We need to discuss how analyzing DNA and proteins helps us understand evolutionary relationships and construct phylogenetic trees. The primary form of molecular evidence comes from comparing the base sequences of DNA or the amino acid sequences of proteins between different organisms. When we compare these sequences, we find striking similarities between distinct species. For example, humans and chimpanzees share a very high percentage of their DNA sequence. These molecular similarities are not coincidental; they provide strong evidence for common ancestry . The logic is simple: species have similar genetic codes because they inherited them from a shared ancestor. Over time, as populations separate and evolve, mutations occur, but the core sequence remains similar. Scientists use this molecular data to construct phylogenetic trees (or cladograms). These are diagrams that map out the evolutionary pathways, showing which species are most closely related. Species that are grouped toget

questions.correct_answer: Phospholipids have a hydrophilic (polar) head; Phospholipids have hydrophobic (non-polar) tails; In water, phospholipids spontaneously form a bilayer; Hydrophobic tails face inward and hydrophilic heads face outward toward the aqueous environment
questions.explanation: To understand how phospholipids form membranes, we first look at their chemical nature. Phospholipids are amphipathic , meaning they have two distinct regions with opposite properties: a hydrophilic (water-loving) part and a hydrophobic (water-fearing) part. This concept is a prerequisite covered in Topic B1.1: Carbohydrates and lipids , specifically regarding the hydrophobic properties of lipids. The "head" of the phospholipid molecule contains a phosphate group. Because this group is polar/charged, it is hydrophilic . This allows the head to form hydrogen bonds with water molecules (H 2 O). Attached to the head are two long hydrocarbon chains known as fatty acid tails . These chains are non-polar and hydrophobic , meaning they do not dissolve in water and instead repel it. When phospholipids are placed in an aqueous (water-based) environment, they spontaneously arrange themselves to find the most stable energetic state. To minimize the contact between the hydrophobic tails and water, the molecules organize into a double layer , or bilayer . questions.explanation: Let's start by looking at Protein A . The table shows it has a very high hydrophobic amino acid content of 75%. Because its primary location is the Cell Membrane , this composition makes perfect sense. As you might remember from Topic B2.1 (Membranes) , cell membranes are made of a phospholipid bilayer with a non-polar, hydrophobic core. For a protein to be stable within this environment, it needs a high percentage of hydrophobic amino acids to interact with the fatty acid tails of the lipids. Next, let's look at Protein B . It is located in the Cytoplasm and has a higher hydrophilic content (60%) compared to Protein A. The cytoplasm is an aqueous (water-based) environment. According to the solvent properties of water covered in Topic A1.1 , substances must be polar or charged to remain soluble in water. Therefore, Protein B requires a higher percentage of hydrophilic amino acids on its surface to function effectively in the watery environment of the cell. Finally, we examine Protein C , which is found in the Extracellular Fluid . This protein has the highest hydrophilic content at 80%. questions.explanation: According to the table, Protein A is located in the Cell Membrane . Using the Environmental Matching Approach , we first look at the chemical nature of this specific environment. In Topic B1.1 (Carbohydrates and lipids) , we learn that cell membranes are primarily composed of a phospholipid bilayer. A phospholipid bilayer has a unique structure: it has a hydrophobic (water-fearing) core formed by fatty acid tails. This is a key concept from the syllabus: - Syllabus B1.1.8 : Hydrophobic properties of lipids. - Syllabus B1.1.12 : Formation of phospholipid bilayers. Because the interior of the membrane is non-polar, any molecule residing there must be chemically compatible with that non-polar environment. For Protein A to remain stable within the membrane, its amino acids must "match" the hydrophobicity of the lipid tails. As noted in Topic B1.2.10 , the effect of non-polar (hydrophobic) amino acids is crucial for the tertiary structure and placement of proteins. Having a high percentage (75%) of hydrophobic amino acids ensures that the protein can form strong hydrophobic interactions with the lipid bilayer, allowing it to remain securely embedded in the membrane rather than being pus

questions.question_text: Compare the form and function of α-keratin and insulin, explaining why each protein's structure is suited to its role in the body.
questions.correct_answer: α-Keratin: fibrous, structural role in hair, nails, skin; strong and insoluble; Insulin: globular, soluble, acts as hormone in bloodstream; Shape supports function: keratin provides strength; insulin enables receptor binding; 3 marks total
questions.explanation: To compare these two proteins, we first categorize them based on their overall 3D conformation. * α-keratin is a fibrous protein , characterized by long, narrow, and repetitive sequences. * Insulin is a globular protein , which has a compact, rounded, and complex tertiary structure. This fundamental difference in shape is the basis for their different roles in the body, as covered in Topic B1.2: Proteins . A key attribute to contrast is how these proteins interact with water: * Solubility : α-keratin is insoluble in water. This is essential because it forms external structures like hair and skin that must remain intact when wet. In contrast, insulin is soluble , allowing it to dissolve in the blood plasma for transport throughout the body. * Stability : The fibrous nature of keratin (held together by many hydrogen and disulfide bonds, as seen in the figure) makes it very strong and resistant to change. Insulin, being globular, is more chemically sensitive but highly specific in its shape to allow for molecular recognition. Finally, we look at how their forms dictate their functions: * α-Keratin (Structural Role) : Its long, fibrous filaments provide mechanical strength and protecti

Topic: B2.1 Membranes and membrane transport, B2.2 Organelles and compartmentalization Section B: Up to one additional mark is available for the construction of your answers for each question.

Analyze the specific roles played by cholesterol and glycoproteins in maintaining the integrity and function of the plasma membrane.
questions.correct_answer: Cholesterol is an amphipathic molecule that embeds within the hydrophobic tail region of the phospholipid bilayer; It regulates membrane fluidity by restricting the movement of phospholipids at high temperatures; It prevents the membrane from solidifying/crystallizing at low temperatures by disrupting the regular packing of hydrocarbon chains; Glycoproteins consist of carbohydrate chains covalently bonded to proteins on the extracellular surface; They serve as cell-to-cell recognition markers (e.g., identifying self vs. non-self in the immune system); They act as receptors for chemical signals such as hormones or neurotransmitters; They are involved in cell adhesion, helping cells stick together to form tissues; <note>Award maximum 4 marks</note>

questions.question_text: Detail the sequence of events in a single cycle of the sodium-potassium (Na+/K+) pump and explain how this contributes to the cell's electrochemical gradient.
questions.correct_answer: The pump is an integral transmembrane protein with high affinity for sodium ions in its internal configuration; Three sodium ions (3Na<sup>+</sup>) bind to specific binding sites on the intracellular side of the pump; The binding of Na<sup>+</sup> triggers the hydrolysis of ATP, which phosphorylates the pump (attaches a phosphate group); Phosphorylation causes a conformational change (shape change) in the protein, translocating the Na<sup>+</sup> across the membrane; The 3Na<sup>+</sup> ions are released to the extracellular fluid, and the pump now has a high affinity for potassium ions; Two potassium ions (2K<sup>+</sup>) bind to the pump from the extracellular side, triggering the release of the phosphate group; Dephosphorylation causes the pump to return to its original conformation, releasing the 2K<sup>+</sup> into the cytoplasm; Because more positive charge is moved out (3Na<sup>+</sup>) than in (2K<sup>+</sup>), the pump is electrogenic and establishes a negative internal membrane potential; <note>Award maximum 7 marks</note>

questions.question_text: Explain how the fluidity of the phospholipid bilayer enables the processes of endocytosis and exocytosis.
questions.correct_answer: The fluid nature of the membrane is due to the weak hydrophobic interactions between the fatty acid tails, allowing phospholipids to move laterally; This flexibility allows the plasma membrane to change shape and invaginate to form vesicles during endocytosis; During exocytosis, the phospholipid bilayers of the secretory vesicle and the plasma membrane can merge/fuse because they are both fluid; Fusion is followed by the spontaneous rearrangement of the bilayer to become continuous, releasing the vesicle's contents; Fluidity ensures that the membrane can break and reform (re-seal) without losing its integrity or leaking cytoplasm; <note>Award maximum 4 marks</note>

questions.explanation: This question asks us to describe how temperature and pH influence the permeability of cell membranes. To earn full marks, we need to address both high and low extremes for temperature and explain the impact of pH on the membrane's components, such as proteins and lipids. This topic is covered in Topic B2.1: Membranes and membrane transport and Topic B1.2: Proteins . Understanding the fluid mosaic model is essential here. When temperature increases, the kinetic energy of the phospholipid molecules in the bilayer also increases. This leads to more movement and a higher state of fluidity . As the phospholipids move further apart, the membrane becomes more porous or "leaky," which increases its permeability . This allows substances to pass through more easily than they would at lower temperatures. Conversely, at low temperatures, phospholipids have less kinetic energy and pack more closely together. This makes the membrane more rigid and less fluid. In this state, the membrane acts as a more effective barrier, which reduces its permeability . The molecules are so tightly packed that it is difficult for substances to diffuse across the bilayer. Cell membranes contain many integral and

questions.question_text: Explain the role of cholesterol in maintaining the fluidity of the membrane.
questions.correct_answer: Cholesterol is interspersed between fatty acid tails of the phospholipid bilayer; Prevents fatty acid chains from packing too closely together in cold temperatures, maintaining membrane fluidity; Restrains movement of fatty acid chains in high temperatures, preventing excessive fluidity; Ensures the membrane remains flexible and functional across temperature variations; [Total: 4 marks]
questions.explanation: To understand how cholesterol works, we first look at where it is located. In animal cell membranes, cholesterol is an amphipathic molecule found interspersed between the fatty acid tails of the phospholipid bilayer. Its hydrophobic steroid rings sit among the hydrocarbon tails, while its tiny hydrophilic hydroxyl (-OH) group aligns with the phosphate heads of the phospholipids. In cold environments, phospholipids naturally lose kinetic energy and tend to cluster together, which could cause the membrane to solidify into a rigid, crystalline state. Cholesterol acts as a physical spacer. By being wedged between the tails, it prevents the fatty acid chains from packing too closely together , which maintains membrane fluidity even when it's cold. Conversely, at high temperatures, phospholipids move more rapidly, which can make the membrane too liquid or "leaky." Cholesterol's rigid ring structure helps restrain the movement of the fatty acid chains . It essentially pulls the tails together, increasing the membrane's stability and preventing it from becoming excessively fluid. Because cholesterol has these two opposing effects, it is often called a "fluidity buffer." Its presence ensure

questions.explanation: In biology, we often use the phrase "form follows function." This means that the physical structure (form) of a cell is specifically adapted to perform a certain job (function). In multicellular organisms, cells undergo differentiation to become specialized, developing unique features that make them highly efficient at a particular task. Let's look at nerve cells (neurons) . Another classic example is the red blood cell (erythrocyte) , which is responsible for transporting oxygen. Its form is perfectly specialized for this: * Biconcave Shape: Instead of being a simple sphere, it is a flattened disc indented on both sides. questions.explanation: To understand how a neuron works, we follow the electrical impulse in one direction: from the receiving end to the sending end. This process is covered in Topic C2.2: Neural signalling . The specialized structures of the neuron ensure that the signal is received, integrated, and then sent quickly over long distances. The journey begins at the dendrites . These are thin, branch-like extensions that increase the surface area of the neuron. Their specialized structure allows them to receive incoming signals from other neurons and transmit those signals toward the cell body. The signal moves to the cell body (or soma). This is the metabolic center of the neuron. Its role is to integrate signals from all the various dendrites. If the combined signal is strong enough to reach a certain threshold, the cell body generates an action potential (the electrical impulse) at the start of the axon. Once generated, the electrical signal travels down the axon . The axon is a long, thin fiber specifically adapted to conduct electrical signals over long distances throughout the body without losing signal strength. questions.explanation: In a multicellular organism, not every cell needs to do every job. Instead, the organism uses a division of labor . This means that different cell types are assigned specific roles. By focusing on a single task, these cells can perform their functions much more effectively than a "generalized" cell that tries to do everything at once. A generalized unicellular organism must carry out all life processes (metabolism, response, homeostasis, etc.) within one cell. In contrast, specialized cells in multicellular organisms can devote their entire energy budget and internal machinery to one specific function. This focus results in a much higher level of efficiency for that particular task. To be efficient, specialized cells develop unique physical structures or chemical compositions. For example: * Nerve cells (neurons): Have long axons to transmit electrical signals over great distances quickly. * Muscle cells: Contain high concentrations of contractile proteins (actin and myosin) for movement. * Red blood cells: Lack a nucleus to maximize space for hemoglobin, allowing for efficient oxygen transport. questions.question_text: Based on Figures a and b, outline the sequence of events by which central chemoreceptors coordinate the feedback control of ventilation rate during hypercapnia.
questions.correct_answer: CO<sub>2</sub> diffuses into CSF; central chemoreceptors detect rise in H<sup>+</sup>; Send afferent signals to medulla; medulla integrates input; Sends efferent signals to respiratory muscles (diaphragm, intercostals); Ventilation rate increases to remove excess CO<sub>2</sub>
questions.explanation: To understand how the body responds to hypercapnia (an increase in blood CO 2 levels), we first look at the chemical environment of the brain. CO 2 is a lipid-soluble gas that easily diffuses out of the blood and across the blood-brain barrier into the Cerebrospinal Fluid (CSF) . Once inside the CSF, CO 2 reacts with water to form hydrogen ions (H + ) and bicarbonate. This makes the CSF more acidic (lowers the pH). The central chemoreceptors (located near the surface of the medulla) are specifically sensitive to this increase in H + concentration. This is the first mark-earning step in the biological sequence. When the chemoreceptors detect high H + levels, they send afferent (sensory) nerve impulses to the respiratory control center in the medulla . The medulla acts as the integration center, processing these signals to determine that the current ventilation rate is insufficient to maintain homeostasis. The medulla then sends efferent (motor) signals through the phrenic and intercostal nerves. These signals travel to the respiratory muscles , specifically the diaphragm and the intercostal muscles. questions.explanation: To understand why muscles work in pairs, we have to look at their mechanical logic: muscles can only exert force by contracting (pulling). They cannot 'push' a structure back to its original position. Because the ribcage needs to move in two opposite directions to facilitate breathing, it requires two sets of muscles pulling in opposite directions. The external and internal intercostal muscles form an antagonistic pair. In the IB Biology syllabus, specifically in Topic B3.3 (Muscle and motility) , we learn that these muscles have opposing effects on the ribcage: - External intercostals: Contract to pull the ribcage upward and outward (inspiration). - Internal intercostals: Contract to pull the ribcage downward and inward (forced expiration). Since a muscle cannot push, the external intercostals cannot move the ribs back down; the internal intercostals must 'take over' the pulling work to reverse the movement. questions.explanation: The process begins in the Sinoatrial (SA) node , which is a specialized group of cells located in the wall of the right atrium. This node acts as the heart's natural pacemaker by spontaneously generating electrical impulses without needing a signal from the brain (this property is known as being myogenic ). This first impulse sets the rhythm for the entire heart cycle. Once the SA node fires, the electrical signal spreads rapidly through the muscle walls of both the left and right atria. This electrical stimulation causes the atria to contract simultaneously (atrial systole), which pushes blood through the open valves into the ventricles below. The electrical impulse reaches a second "gateway" called the Atrioventricular (AV) node , located in the lower part of the right atrium near the border with the ventricles. A crucial event happens here: the AV node delays the impulse for about 0.1 seconds. This pause is vital because it ensures the atria have completely finished contracting and the ventricles are fully filled with blood before they start to squeeze. questions.question_text: Explain how the root system of a cactus is adapted for obtaining water.

questions.question_text: Explain how adaptive radiation allows species to occupy different ecological niches in an isolated environment.
questions.correct_answer: Adaptive radiation is the process where organisms diversify rapidly into multiple new forms; This occurs when environmental changes create new resources, challenges, or open new niches; In isolated environments (e.g., islands), populations can adapt to different ecological niches; Physical traits develop differently in response to environmental pressures; Example: finches develop different beak sizes/shapes to exploit different food sources; These adaptations reduce competition between populations; Allows more efficient use of available resources; Over time, these adaptations can lead to formation of new species; <note>Award marks for other relevant examples of adaptive radiation if provided</note>
questions.explanation: Adaptive radiation is an evolutionary process where a single ancestral species diversifies rapidly into a wide variety of new forms. This typically occurs when a change in the environment makes new resources available or opens up new ecological niches. In the IB curriculum, this is often discussed in Topic A4.1: Evolution and speciation . The process often begins with geographical isolation . A small population of an ancestral species reaches an isolated environment, such as an island chain (archipelago) or a remote lake. Because they are physically separated from the original population, gene flow is restricted, allowing the isolated groups to evolve independently. Within these isolated environments, different populations encounter varied selection pressures . For example, one island might have an abundance of large, hard seeds, while another has many flowering plants with deep nectar wells. These represent different ecological niches —the specific functional roles and habitats of a species. In response to these specific pressures, natural selection favors individuals with heritable traits that best suit their particular niche. Over many generations, phenotypic divergence occurs a

In a graph of product concentration against time, the gradient represents the rate of reaction: Rate = fracΔ [Product]Δ t Comparing the "Competitive Inhibitor" curve to the "Control" curve, we can see that the slope is shallower for the inhibitor during this initial period. Because the gradient of the competitive inhibitor curve is less steep than the control, we can conclude that the presence of the inhibitor causes a decrease in the speed of the reaction. In IB Biology, it is crucial to specify that this is the initial rate of reaction that is being affected. This slower rate occurs because a competitive inhibitor has a chemical structure similar to the substrate. As a result, it competes with the substrate to bind to the active site of the enzyme. Instead, it binds to a specific location on the enzyme known as the allosteric site . When the inhibitor binds to this allosteric site, it causes a conformational change in the protein. This means the overall three-dimensional shape of the enzyme molecule is altered or distorted. Because the enzyme's structure is shifted, the shape of the active site changes as well. It is no longer complementary to the substrate, meaning the substrate can no longer bind to the enzyme to undergo a reaction. questions.question_text: Outline how RuBP is regenerated in the Calvin cycle and explain why this regeneration is necessary.
questions.correct_answer: Triose phosphate (TP) / glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate (G3P) is converted into ribulose-5-phosphate.; ATP is used to phosphorylate ribulose-5-phosphate.; Resulting in the formation of ribulose 1,5-bisphosphate (RuBP).; RuBP is the initial carbon dioxide acceptor in the Calvin cycle.; Regeneration ensures the continuous availability of RuBP.; This allows the Calvin cycle to continue / sustain carbon fixation / synthesize glucose.; <Note>Accept labeled diagram alongside explanation</Note>
questions.explanation: To understand how RuBP is regenerated, we first need to look at the product of the reduction phase in the Calvin cycle. The cycle produces triose phosphate (TP) , also known as glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate (G3P). While some TP is used to synthesize glucose and other organic compounds, the majority of it must be recycled to keep the cycle turning. This process takes place in the stroma of the chloroplast. The first phase of regeneration involves a complex series of enzymatic reactions that rearrange the carbon skeletons of the triose phosphate molecules. Through these reactions, the 3-carbon TP molecules are converted into 5-carbon molecules called ribulose-5-phosphate . Once ribulose-5-phosphate is formed, it must be "activated" to become the high-energy CO 2 acceptor. ATP (produced during the light-dependent reactions) is used to phosphorylate ribulose-5-phosphate. questions.explanation: To describe the relationship, we first look at how cAMP production changes as we add more ligand. For example, at 5 nM, production is 3.8 pmol min -1 , but it jumps to 15.2 pmol min -1 when the concentration reaches 25 nM. However, between 50 nM and 100 nM, the production only increases by a tiny amount (0.5 pmol min -1 ), indicating that the system has reached a plateau. In IB Biology, this concept is explored in Topic C2.1: Chemical Signalling , where we study how receptors transition from an inactive to an active state upon binding a ligand. Using the Receptor Saturation Approach , we focus on the physical occupancy of the receptors. Every cell has a finite (limited) number of G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) on its membrane. When the ligand concentration is very high (exceeding 50 nM), every available receptor binding site becomes occupied by a ligand. At this point, the receptors are said to be saturated . Since all receptors are already bound to ligands, adding even more ligand molecules has no effect because there are no "empty" receptors left to receive the signal. questions.explanation: Even when a neuron is not firing an action potential, small amounts of neurotransmitter are occasionally released into the synaptic cleft. As shown in Panel C , this is called spontaneous release . Unlike 'evoked' release, which is a massive surge triggered by a signal, spontaneous release is a quiet, continuous process. From a physiological maintenance perspective, synapses require a constant 'trickle' of activity to remain healthy and stable. This baseline synaptic activity prevents the synapse from becoming dormant. Without this low-level stimulation, the post-synaptic receptors might degrade or the connection might weaken over time. Spontaneous release also ensures synaptic readiness . By having vesicles occasionally dock, prime, and fuse (as seen in Panel A ), the molecular machinery remains active and 'warmed up.' This ensures that when a real action potential finally arrives, the synapse is prepared to respond immediately and efficiently. According to the markscheme, you only need to provide one reason. questions.explanation: Intact skin and mucous membranes act as non-specific physical (and chemical) barriers that prevent pathogen entry.

questions.question_text: The diagram below shows the blood clotting process. What is the role of platelets in this process?
questions.correct_answer: Triggering clot formation by releasing clotting factors
choices: Triggering clot formation by releasing clotting factors
Absorbing excess fluid from the wound
Inhibiting blood flow to the injury

questions.question_text:
Which row correctly describes the roles of the skin and mucous membranes in protecting the body from infection?

SkinMucous membranes
AForms a keratinized physical barrier against pathogens.Produces a sticky fluid that traps microorganisms.
BSecretes mucus to neutralize incoming toxins.Forms a tough, dry, and waterproof outer layer.
CForms a keratinized physical barrier against pathogens.Contains phagocytic cells that engulf pathogens.
DProvides a porous surface for the exchange of microbes.Secretes a layer of acid that dissolves fungal spores.
questions.correct_answer: A

questions.question_text:
A vaccine containing an attenuated (weakened) virus is administered. In a separate situation, an emergency injection of antivenom consisting of concentrated antibodies is administered.

Which row in the table correctly classifies the types of immunity provided by these two medical interventions?

VaccinationAntivenom injection
AArtificial activeArtificial passive
BArtificial passiveArtificial active
CNatural activeNatural passive
DArtificial activeNatural active
questions.correct_answer: A
questions.explanation: Artificial active immunity is acquired via a vaccine (stimulating the body's own immune response), whereas artificial passive immunity is the transfer of ready-made antibodies (antivenom).

questions.question_text:
The human body has several non-specific (innate) defence mechanisms that reduce the chance of infection by pathogens.

Outline what is meant by primary defence.
questions.correct_answer: Primary defence is the body’s first line of defence (non-specific/innate) that prevents the entry of pathogens.; Consists of physical and chemical barriers.; Acts before internal immune responses are activated.; Accept examples such as skin/mucous membranes/secretions as part of this first line.

questions.question_text: Describe the role of skin and sebaceous glands in defence against pathogens.
questions.correct_answer: Skin forms a physical barrier to pathogen entry (keratinised epidermis/tight junctions).; Continuous shedding/removal of skin cells reduces colonisation.; Sebaceous glands secrete sebum.; Sebum is acidic/contains antimicrobial substances and inhibits growth of microorganisms.; Accept that reduced water availability on skin surface limits microbial growth.

questions.question_text: Explain how mucous membranes protect the body from pathogens.
questions.correct_answer: Mucous membranes line body passages/cavities (e.g. respiratory/digestive/urogenital), forming a protective surface.; Goblet cells secrete mucus that traps pathogens/particles.; Cilia move mucus to remove trapped pathogens (mucociliary escalator) and it is swallowed/expelled.; Mucus contains antimicrobial chemicals/enzymes (e.g. lysozyme) that damage microbes.; Secretions can contain antibodies (IgA) that neutralise pathogens.; Keeping surfaces moist reduces cracking and maintains barrier function.; Prevents pathogens reaching underlying tissues/bloodstream, reducing likelihood of infection.

questions.question_text:
The table below summarizes the biochemical cascade that leads to the formation of a blood clot after a skin injury.

StageEvent
IDamaged tissue and platelets release clotting factors
IIClotting factors convert the inactive protein prothrombin into the enzyme thrombin
IIIX
IVAn insoluble mesh of fibers traps blood cells to form a stable clot

Which of the following describes the event that occurs at stage X?
questions.correct_answer: Thrombin catalyzes the conversion of soluble fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin
choices: Thrombin is converted into fibrinogen by the action of platelets
Fibrinogen catalyzes the conversion of prothrombin into active thrombin
Thrombin catalyzes the conversion of soluble fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin
Insoluble fibrin is broken down into soluble prothrombin to dissolve the clot

questions.question_text:
The table below shows the concentration of specific antibodies in a person's blood following two separate exposures to the same pathogen.

Time (days)EventAntibody concentration (μg mL-1)
0First exposure0
10Peak of primary response12
20Monitoring phase4
30Second exposure2
40Peak of secondary response380

Which of the following best accounts for the data recorded between day 30 and day 40?
questions.correct_answer: Memory cells produced during the first exposure rapidly divide and differentiate into antibody-secreting plasma cells.
choices: Antigens from the first exposure are stored in the spleen and released in large quantities during the second exposure.
Non-specific phagocytes 'remember' the surface proteins of the pathogen and begin producing antibodies more efficiently.
Memory cells produced during the first exposure rapidly divide and differentiate into antibody-secreting plasma cells.
The body increases the production of natural antibiotics which work to stimulate the existing pool of antibodies.

questions.question_text: Explain how natural selection leads to the development of antibiotic resistance in bacteria.
questions.correct_answer: Antibiotic resistance in bacteria is a result of natural selection.; When a population of bacteria is exposed to an antibiotic, most of the bacteria are killed.; Some bacteria may have mutations that make them resistant to the drug.; These resistant bacteria survive and reproduce.; They pass on the resistance genes to their offspring.; <note>Maximum 3 marks</note>

questions.question_text: Suggest two ways in which antibiotic resistance genes can spread between bacteria.
questions.correct_answer: Resistance genes can be transferred by conjugation via a plasmid between bacterial cells.; Resistance genes can be transferred by transformation when bacteria take up DNA from the environment.; _OR_; Resistance genes can be transferred by transduction via bacteriophages.; Resistance genes can be transferred by conjugation via plasmids.; Maximum 2 marks

questions.question_text: Why do antibiotics fail to control viral infections?
questions.correct_answer: Viruses lack the cell structures that antibiotics target
choices: Viruses lack the cell structures that antibiotics target
Viruses produce enzymes that degrade antibiotics
Antibiotics block the viral replication process

questions.question_text:
The table shows properties of various cell types involved in the immune response and biotechnology. Which row represents the characteristics of a hybridoma cell used in the commercial production of monoclonal antibodies?

Type of antibody producedDivision capacity in culture
AMonoclonalIndefinite
BPolyclonalIndefinite
CMonoclonalLimited
DPolyclonalLimited
questions.correct_answer: A

questions.question_text: What is non-specific immunity to disease?
questions.correct_answer: Endocytosis of pathogens by white blood cells
choices: Endocytosis of pathogens by white blood cells

questions.question_text: What are three major categories of disease cause?
questions.correct_answer: Genetic, environmental, infectious
questions.explanation: These are broad categories of disease cause: inherited (genetic) factors, environmental exposures, and infectious pathogens.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is true regarding HIV transmission?
questions.correct_answer: It can only be transmitted through contact with infected body fluids
choices: It can be transmitted through the air
It can only be transmitted through contact with infected body fluids
It can be transmitted through casual contact with an infected person
It can only be transmitted from mother to child

questions.question_text: In the laboratory production of monoclonal antibodies, a myeloma cell is used to create a hybridoma. What is the main contribution of the myeloma cell to the hybridoma?
questions.correct_answer: It enables the hybridoma to divide and multiply indefinitely.
choices: It provides the organelles necessary for the secretion of the antibodies.
It contains the genetic code for the specific antibody's variable region.
It enables the hybridoma to divide and multiply indefinitely.
It stimulates the fusion of multiple B-lymphocytes into a single clone.

questions.question_text: Which of the following determines the species-specific nature of certain pathogens?
questions.correct_answer: The presence of specific surface receptors on the host's cells
choices: The number of helper T cells activated during the primary infection
The presence of specific surface receptors on the host's cells
The ability of the pathogen to evade the host's immune system by antigenic variation
The rate of histamine release during an allergic response
questions.explanation: Species specificity (host range) is often determined by whether the pathogen can bind to specific receptor molecules on host cell membranes to enter or infect cells.

questions.question_text: Which part of the immune response is illustrated by the following diagram?
questions.correct_answer: Cellular immunity

questions.question_text: State one function of T-helper cells in the immune response.
questions.correct_answer: Activate other immune cells (e.g. B cells, cytotoxic T cells, macrophages) / coordinate immune response

questions.question_text: Outline how T-helper cells are activated by antigen-presenting cells (APCs).
questions.correct_answer: T-helper cells have receptors that recognize a specific antigen presented on MHC class II molecules of an APC; Binding (and co-stimulation) activates the T-helper cell

questions.question_text: Explain how activated T-helper cells coordinate the immune response to a pathogen.
questions.correct_answer: Activated T-helper cells secrete cytokines / interleukins; Cytokines stimulate B cells to proliferate and differentiate into plasma cells to produce antibodies; Cytokines enhance activation/proliferation of cytotoxic T cells and/or activation of macrophages (increasing cell-mediated killing)

Describe the trend in antibody concentration over time after infection.
questions.correct_answer: Antibody concentration starts at 0 μg mL<sup>-1</sup> at day 0.; It increases from day 5 to day 20, peaking at 30 μg mL<sup>-1</sup>.; After day 20, antibody concentration declines (e.g. to 10 μg mL<sup>-1</sup> by day 40).; : increase to a peak (with time frame/data), decrease after the peak (with time frame/data)

questions.question_text: Explain how this data demonstrates the role of the immune system in defense against viral infections.
questions.correct_answer: The adaptive immune response produces specific IgG antibodies after exposure to viral antigens.; The delay to the peak (around day 20) reflects time needed for clonal selection/expansion and differentiation of B cells into plasma cells.; After the peak, antibody concentration declines as antigen is cleared and short-lived plasma cells die; memory B cells persist enabling a faster secondary response.; : antibodies produced by B cells/adaptive response to antigen, time lag/peak explained by clonal expansion and/or memory/secondary response idea

questions.question_text: Which of the following describes the cellular mechanism by which HIV leads to a failure of the immune system?
questions.correct_answer: It causes the depletion of helper T-cells, which are needed to trigger a specific immune response.
choices: It causes the depletion of helper T-cells, which are needed to trigger a specific immune response.
It destroys the cilia in the respiratory tract, allowing pathogens to enter the lungs.
It stimulates the liver to stop producing plasma proteins such as fibrinogen.
It targets and kills memory cells, causing the loss of all previous vaccinations.

questions.question_text: Describe how vaccines work to protect individuals from infectious diseases.
questions.correct_answer: Vaccines stimulate the immune system to recognize and fight pathogens (such as viruses or bacteria); Vaccines contain antigens (parts of the pathogen, or a weakened/inactivated form of the pathogen); Antigens trigger an immune response without causing the disease; This immune response leads to the production of memory cells; Memory cells remain in the body and provide long-term immunity; Memory cells recognize and respond more rapidly and effectively to future exposures to the pathogen; Award [1] for each of the following points up to [4 max]:

questions.question_text: How does HIV affect the immune system adversely?
questions.correct_answer: Progressive reduction in the number of active lymphocytes
choices: Progressive reduction in the number of active lymphocytes
Rapid production of a clone of plasma cells

questions.question_text:
The human body possesses complex biological mechanisms to prevent the entry of pathogens and to respond with high specificity when an infection occurs.

Compare the roles of the skin and mucous membranes as the first line of defence against infectious diseases.
questions.correct_answer: Skin acts as a continuous, tough physical barrier (keratinized layer) while mucous membranes are thinner and found at body openings; Skin produces sebum which lowers the pH to inhibit bacterial growth; Mucous membranes secrete sticky mucus to trap pathogens; Mucus often contains lysozyme, an enzyme that chemically destroys bacterial cell walls; Cilia on some mucous membranes move trapped pathogens out of the body (e.g., trachea); <sub>A</sub>ward maximum 4 marks._

questions.question_text: Explain the sequence of events that prevents pathogens from entering the blood system following a laceration of the skin.
questions.correct_answer: Blood vessels constrict at the site of damage to reduce blood loss; Platelets adhere to exposed collagen at the wound site and form a temporary platelet plug; Damaged tissues and platelets release clotting factors (thromboplastin); Calcium ions are required for activation of clotting factors in the cascade; The inactive plasma protein prothrombin is converted into the active enzyme thrombin; Thrombin catalyzes the conversion of soluble fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin; Fibrin forms a mesh/network of fibers that traps blood cells to form a semi-solid clot/scab, sealing the wound and reducing pathogen entry; <sub>A</sub>ward maximum 4 marks._

questions.question_text: Explain how antibodies contribute to medical diagnostics.
questions.correct_answer: Antibodies bind specifically to their antigen/epitope; Antibodies can be immobilised on a solid support (e.g., membrane/well) to capture antigen from a sample; A second antibody with a label (e.g., enzyme/fluorophore/coloured particle) can bind to form an antigen–antibody complex (sandwich assay); The label produces a detectable signal (colour change/fluorescence) indicating presence of the target molecule; Quantity of signal can be proportional to antigen concentration (semi-quantitative/quantitative tests); Example: pregnancy tests use antibodies to detect the hormone hCG in urine; Example: antibodies are used in ELISA/rapid tests to diagnose infection by detecting pathogen antigens or patient antibodies

questions.question_text:
A researcher uses a replica plating technique to study the emergence of drug resistance in Staphylococcus aureus. A master plate containing 300 colonies grown on nutrient agar is transferred to three separate replica plates containing the antibiotic erythromycin. The results are recorded in the table below:

PlateCulture MediumColony CountPattern of Growth
MasterNutrient Agar300Randomly distributed colonies
Replica 1Agar + Erythromycin4Colonies at positions P, Q, R, and S
Replica 2Agar + Erythromycin4Colonies at positions P, Q, R, and S
Replica 3Agar + Erythromycin4Colonies at positions P, Q, R, and S

What conclusion about the origin of antibiotic resistance is best supported by these results?
questions.correct_answer: Resistance-conferring mutations occurred randomly before the bacteria were exposed to the antibiotic.
choices: The antibiotic environment triggered the specific mutations required for the bacteria to survive.
Resistance-conferring mutations occurred randomly before the bacteria were exposed to the antibiotic.
The colonies grew because they were able to adapt their metabolic pathways to use the antibiotic as a carbon source.
Resistant traits are only passed to the next generation if the parent cell detects the antibiotic in its immediate surroundings.

questions.question_text:
A lab experiment investigates how increasing doses of a foreign protein antigen affect antibody production in test animals. Antibody concentrations were measured at Day 3 and Day 7 post-injection.

Table: Antibody concentration following antigen administration

Antigen dose / μg mL-1Antibody concentration (Day 3) / μg mL-1Antibody concentration (Day 7) / μg mL-1
00.00.0
0.10.51.2
0.52.13.5
13.85.9
25.27.5
55.88.2
105.98.3

Using both the table and the graph, at what antigen dose does the antibody concentration plateau?
questions.correct_answer: About 5–10 μg mL<sup>-1</sup> (little/no further increase beyond 5 μg mL<sup>-1</sup>)

questions.question_text: Compare antibody concentrations on Day 3 and Day 7 across the antigen doses.
questions.correct_answer: At every non-zero antigen dose, Day 7 antibody concentration is higher than Day 3; Antibody concentration increases with dose on both days, but Day 7 rises more/has a steeper increase at low–mid doses; The difference between Day 7 and Day 3 is small at very low dose and becomes larger as dose increases (up to the plateau); Both time points show a plateau at higher doses (little change from 5 to 10 μg mL<sup>-1</sup>)

questions.question_text: Using evidence from the data, explain the relationship between antigen dose and immune system activation.
questions.correct_answer: Antibody concentration increases as antigen dose increases (dose-dependent response); Use of data to support (e.g. Day 7: 0.0 at 0 to 8.2 at 5 μg mL-1; Day 3: 0.0 at 0 to 5.8 at 5 μg mL-1); Higher antigen dose increases probability/extent of B-cell activation and clonal expansion, leading to more plasma cells and antibody secretion; Response approaches a maximum at high dose, suggesting limiting factors in activation/production; _OR_; Stated as a “dose-dependent immune response” with appropriate reference to increasing antibody concentrations with increasing dose

questions.question_text: Suggest a biological explanation for why the increase in antibody concentration slows beyond 5 μg mL-1 of antigen.
questions.correct_answer: Finite number of antigen-specific B cells / B-cell response becomes saturated (maximum clonal expansion/plasma cell output reached); Limiting helper T-cell signalling/cytokines or other resources (e.g. nutrients, space in lymphoid tissue) restrict further increase; Negative feedback/immune regulation reduces further activation (e.g. regulatory T cells; antibody–antigen complexes reducing stimulation); Antigen processing/presentation becomes limiting at high antigen levels; _OR_; Memory cell formation shifts response away from further increasing short-term antibody concentration

questions.question_text: Antigens are essential for vaccine development. Suggest how the findings of this experiment could guide the formulation of vaccine doses.
questions.correct_answer: Choose an antigen dose near the point just before/at the plateau (about 5 μg mL<sup>-1</sup>) to achieve a strong antibody response; Avoid higher doses because they produce minimal additional antibody but increase cost/antigen use; Avoid unnecessarily high doses that could increase risk of adverse effects/overstimulation without added benefit

questions.question_text: State one example in which antigens from red blood cells are involved in medical testing or safety.
questions.correct_answer: Blood typing for transfusion safety; _OR_; Rh testing in pregnancy; Accept: Coombs test, cross-matching, etc.

questions.question_text: Describe how macrophages destroy pathogens in the immune system.
questions.correct_answer: Macrophages recognize and bind to pathogens using surface receptors.; Macrophages engulf pathogens through phagocytosis, forming a phagosome.; The phagosome fuses with a lysosome containing digestive enzymes.; The enzymes break down/digest the pathogen's proteins and other components.; The digested material is expelled from the cell by exocytosis.; Some pathogen fragments are presented on the cell surface as antigens to activate T-cells.

questions.question_text: A community in ecology refers to:
questions.correct_answer: All populations living and interacting in an ecosystem
choices: All non-living components of an ecosystem
All populations living and interacting in an ecosystem
A habitat used only by plants

questions.question_text: The Lincoln index is used to estimate populations of which type of organism?
questions.correct_answer: motile organisms
questions.explanation: Correct. The Lincoln index (mark–release–recapture) is used to estimate populations of motile organisms.

questions.question_text:
In a mark–recapture study, the following were recorded:

* M = 24 (initially marked) * n = 60 (total in second capture) * R = 12 (marked in second capture)

What is the estimated population size?
questions.explanation: Use the Lincoln index formula: N = n × M/R N = 60 × 24/12 = 120

questions.question_text: Why is random sampling often used in population studies?
questions.correct_answer: It is quicker and reduces bias compared to full counts
choices: It is quicker and reduces bias compared to full counts

questions.question_text:
A population of wildflowers fluctuates year by year. Quadrat sampling shows lower densities during droughts, followed by recovery.

Which statement best explains this pattern?
questions.correct_answer: Abiotic stress altering sigmoid growth parameters and enhancing density-dependent limits
choices: Sampling error due to a clumped distribution
Abiotic stress altering sigmoid growth parameters and enhancing density-dependent limits
Herbivory increasing growth rates and masking real change
Quadrat size that was too large to detect individual plants

questions.question_text:
In a mark–recapture (Lincoln index) study, the second sample contains fewer marked animals than expected if marked and unmarked individuals have equal probability of capture. Assume the population is closed (no immigration or emigration), no births or deaths occurred, and marks were not lost or missed.

What is the most likely explanation?
questions.correct_answer: Marked individuals avoided the trap after the first capture, so recapture probability was reduced.
choices: Marked individuals avoided the trap after the first capture, so recapture probability was reduced.
The population size increased due to immigration between the two samples.
Marked and unmarked animals did not mix fully before the second sample was taken.
The marks became less visible between samples, so marked animals were recorded as unmarked.
questions.explanation: trap shyness/stress changes capture probability, violating the equal catchability assumption.

questions.question_text:
A species of pine secretes toxins that inhibit the root growth of nearby competing plants. However, fungi living symbiotically on the pine roots are unaffected.

Which statement best describes the ecological interactions shown?
questions.correct_answer: Mutualism and competitive suppression can occur simultaneously.
choices: The pine’s toxins harm its mutualistic fungi, reducing mutualism.
The pine’s allelopathy enhances competition with mutualists.
Mutualism and competitive suppression can occur simultaneously.
Allelopathy only occurs in high-density forests.
questions.explanation: The pine–fungus relationship is mutualism, while toxins suppress nearby competing plants; both interactions coexist.

questions.question_text: What type of interaction is mutualism?
questions.correct_answer: Both species benefit
choices: One species benefits, one is harmed
One species benefits, one is unaffected

questions.question_text:
Garlic mustard is an invasive plant that secretes chemicals toxic to surrounding tree seedlings. A chi-squared test shows a strong negative association between their presence.

What is the best interpretation of this pattern?
questions.correct_answer: A statistically significant association, likely due to allelopathy
choices: A statistically significant association, likely due to allelopathy
Both species rely on the same pollinators
questions.explanation: Correct. A significant negative association is consistent with garlic mustard inhibiting seedling establishment via toxic secretions (allelopathy).

questions.question_text: What happens when a population exceeds carrying capacity?
questions.correct_answer: The death rate tends to increase.
choices: The death rate tends to increase.

questions.question_text: Which of the following best describes a predator–prey relationship?
questions.correct_answer: Prey numbers increase → predator numbers follow → prey numbers drop.
choices: Predator numbers increase → prey numbers decrease → predator numbers then decrease.
Predator and prey populations always remain constant over time.
Predator and prey compete directly for the same food resource.
Prey numbers increase → predator numbers follow → prey numbers drop.

questions.question_text: When applying a chi2 test to two species' distributions, which result most strongly supports a non-random association?
questions.correct_answer: A p-value below 0.05
choices: Observed and expected values are identical

questions.question_text:
A native plant species declines after an invasive plant species spreads. Removal of the invasive plant leads to partial recovery in the native plant population size. A chi-squared test between the species distributions yields p < 0.05.

What is the most reasonable conclusion?
questions.correct_answer: Interspecific competition likely exists between the two plant species
choices: There is strong evidence of mutualism
The species coexist due to shared niches
Interspecific competition likely exists between the two plant species

questions.question_text:
A community contains five species: a grass, a rodent, a hawk, a decomposer, and a parasitic mite. Each plays a different ecological role.

Which interaction represents top-down control?
questions.correct_answer: Hawks limit rodent numbers through predation.
choices: Hawks limit rodent numbers through predation.
Parasitic mites reduce rodent fitness and survival.
Grass provides food for rodents, increasing rodent population size.

questions.question_text: What defines a population in ecology?
questions.correct_answer: A group of organisms of the same species living in the same area at the same time
choices: All the organisms of various species living in a defined area
A group of organisms of the same species living in the same area at the same time
A group of different species living and interacting with each other
A group of organisms that occupy the same trophic level in an ecosystem
questions.explanation: This is the formal definition of a population in the IB Biology syllabus.

questions.question_text:
In an ecological survey, the presence of two species of lichen, Parmelia and Cladonia, was recorded on 100 trees. The results are shown in the contingency table.

Cladonia presentCladonia absentTotal
Parmelia_ present152540

What is the expected frequency of trees containing both species if there is no association between them?

An ecologist is investigating the various organizational levels of a savanna in East Africa. During the study, the following data sets were collected:

Research FocusData Collected

Which ecological term identifies the level of biological organization described in Focus II?
questions.correct_answer: Community

The following data were collected during a study to estimate the population size of a species of ground beetle in a woodland habitat, assuming the population remained closed during the study period.

DescriptionNumber of individuals
Beetles captured, marked and released in first sample60

Explain how population density affects the transmission of infectious diseases.
questions.correct_answer: Higher population density leads to increased contact rates / closer proximity of individuals, increasing the chance of transmission; Pathogens spread more easily in dense populations (e.g., more frequent encounters/shared spaces), so infection can pass through the population more rapidly; Higher density can increase the basic reproductive number (R<sub>0</sub>) / encounter rate, promoting faster outbreaks; Lower density reduces contact rate, so transmission is less likely and outbreaks spread more slowly

questions.question_text: Which of the following describes a mutualistic relationship between two different species?
questions.correct_answer: Both species involved in the interaction receive a benefit.
choices: One species benefits while the other is harmed by the interaction.
One species benefits and the other species is neither helped nor harmed.
Both species involved in the interaction receive a benefit.
Both species are negatively affected as they compete for the same resource.

Describe the relationship between the rabbit and fox populations over time.
questions.correct_answer: Rabbit population rises first and the fox population increases after a time lag (predator population follows prey); As fox numbers increase, rabbit numbers decrease, indicating predation pressure and cyclical fluctuations; Maxima/minima in fox population occur after maxima/minima in rabbit population (phase shift)

questions.question_text: Explain how predator-prey interactions contribute to population fluctuations in this ecosystem.
questions.correct_answer: Increased rabbit abundance provides more food, improving fox survival/reproduction so fox numbers rise; Rising fox numbers increase predation rate on rabbits, causing rabbit numbers to fall; Reduced rabbit numbers lead to food limitation so fox numbers subsequently decline, allowing rabbits to recover and the cycle repeats

questions.question_text:
The table below provides demographic data for a population of prairie dogs observed over a one-year period. At the start of the study, the initial population size was 2,000.

Demographic FactorNumber of Individuals
Natality420
Mortality310
Immigration70
Emigration140

Based on this data, what is the total population size at the conclusion of the year?
questions.explanation: The final population size is determined by adding the net change (gains minus losses) to the initial population size.Net Change = (Natality + Immigration) - (Mortality + Emigration)Net Change = (420 + 70) - (310 + 140) = 490 - 450 = +40Final Population = 2,000 + 40 = 2,040

questions.question_text: Describe the role of antibiotics in controlling bacterial infections.
questions.correct_answer: Antibiotics are substances that kill bacteria or inhibit their growth; They control infections by targeting specific bacterial processes or structures (e.g. cell wall synthesis or protein synthesis); They do not affect viruses because viruses lack the cellular structures and metabolism targeted by antibiotics; [Max 2 marks]

questions.question_text: Explain how antibiotic resistance develops in bacterial populations.
questions.correct_answer: Genetic variation exists in bacterial populations due to mutation or the acquisition of resistance genes (via horizontal gene transfer/plasmids); Antibiotics act as a selective pressure, killing susceptible/non-resistant bacteria; Resistant bacteria survive and reproduce, passing the resistance allele/gene to their offspring; The frequency of the resistant trait increases in the population over time; [Max 2 marks]

questions.question_text:
A team of ecologists surveyed a coastal grassland ecosystem using two methods.

For sessile organisms (clumped grass species), they used random quadrat sampling. They placed 20 quadrats (1 m2 each) randomly across the area and recorded the following counts per quadrat:

14, 17, 12, 15, 18, 10, 13, 15, 16, 19, 14, 11, 15, 17, 13, 14, 12, 18, 16, 15.

For motile organisms (a local crab species), they used a capture-mark-release-recapture approach. On day 1, they captured and marked 80 crabs. On day 2, they captured 100 crabs, of which 20 were marked.

Finally, the researchers noted that the grassy habitat can only sustain a maximum of approximately 250 individual crabs because of limited burrow space, food availability, and competition.

Calculate the mean number of grass individuals per 1 m2 quadrat from the quadrat sampling data.
questions.correct_answer: Mean = 294/20 = 14.7 individuals per 1 m<sup>2</sup> quadrat

questions.question_text: Based on the quadrat data, explain what the standard deviation would tell the researchers about this grass population.
questions.correct_answer: Standard deviation is a measure of spread/variation in the number of grass individuals per quadrat around the mean; Larger standard deviation indicates greater variability between quadrats (some quadrats have many individuals, others few); Smaller standard deviation indicates counts are more similar between quadrats (more uniform distribution across the sampled area); Link to distribution pattern: greater variability is consistent with patchy/clumped distribution; low variability is consistent with a more even distribution; Award up to 2 marks.

questions.question_text: Using the Lincoln index (Lincoln–Petersen estimator), predict the total population size of the crabs.
questions.correct_answer: Identify values: marked on day 1 (M=80), total caught on day 2 (C=100), marked recaptured on day 2 (R=20); Use Lincoln index: N = MC/R; Substitute: N = 80 × 100/20; N = 400 crabs (individuals); Award up to 2 marks.

questions.question_text: List two major assumptions that must hold true for the Lincoln index estimate to be valid.

questions.question_text:
Define the following terms as related to ecosystems:

Gross primary production
questions.correct_answer: Gross primary production is the total amount of energy captured by photosynthesis in a given area and time period, before any is used for respiration.
questions.explanation: To define Gross Primary Production (GPP), we first look at the role of producers (autotrophs). In an ecosystem, these organisms capture solar energy and convert it into chemical energy through the process of photosynthesis . This is the fundamental entry point for energy into almost all food chains, as explored in Topic C4.2: Transfer of energy and matter . Gross Primary Production represents the total rate at which this energy conversion happens. It is the total amount of light energy that is converted to chemical energy (in the form of organic molecules like glucose) by the producers in an ecosystem. To be scientifically precise, we must measure this over a specific area and time period (for example, kJ · m -2 · yr -1 ). The term "Gross" is critical here. It refers to the energy captured before the plants use any of it for their own metabolic needs. Since plants are living organisms, they must perform cell respiration to stay alive, which consumes some of the energy they just produced. GPP is the "paycheck" before taxes (respiration) are taken out. What remains after respiration is called Net Primary Production (NPP). Based on the markscheme requirements, the full definition is:

In the DNA double helix, Adenine (A) always pairs with Thymine (T), and Cytosine (C) always pairs with Guanine (G). This means that the sequence on one strand automatically dictates the sequence on the other. The physical reason these bases pair so specifically is due to the formation of hydrogen bonds . - A and T form two hydrogen bonds. - C and G form three hydrogen bonds. The chemical structure and the arrangement of polar groups on these nitrogenous bases ensure that only the correct "partner" fits. This molecular specificity prevents mismatches because a different pairing (like A with G) would not align properly to form stable bonds. During replication, the DNA molecule unzips. Each original strand acts as a template . Because of the strict pairing rules, the new strand being built must be complementary to the template strand. If the template has an A, the molecular machinery effectively forces a T into the opposite position. The enzyme DNA polymerase is responsible for catalyzing the formation of the new strand. questions.explanation: To understand how replication works, we first need to recognize that DNA is a double helix where the two strands are antiparallel . This means that one strand runs in a 5' → 3' direction, while the complementary strand runs in the opposite 3' → 5' direction. The central constraint of DNA replication is the specific requirement of the enzyme DNA polymerase . It can only add new nucleotides to the 3' end of a growing DNA strand. Consequently, new DNA can only ever be synthesized in a 5' → 3' direction. Because the template strands are antiparallel, the replication fork opens in a way that allows one strand to be synthesized smoothly. This is the leading strand . DNA polymerase follows the helicase as it unwinds the DNA, adding nucleotides continuously in the 5' → 3' direction toward the replication fork. On the other template strand, the 5' → 3' synthesis must move away from the replication fork. This creates a logistical problem: as the fork opens further, new template becomes available 'behind' the polymerase. This is known as the lagging strand . questions.explanation: DNA polymerase III can only add new nucleotides to the 3' end of a growing DNA strand. This means that DNA synthesis always occurs in a 5' to 3' direction . Because DNA strands are antiparallel , the two template strands run in opposite directions. For the leading strand , the 3' end of the new strand points towards the replication fork . This allows DNA polymerase III to extend the strand continuously as helicase unwinds the DNA. For the lagging strand , the 3' end of the new strand points away from the replication fork . As the fork opens, DNA polymerase III must work in short bursts, moving away from the fork. This results in discontinuous synthesis, creating the fragments shown in Figure 2. In summary, the requirement to add to the 3' end means that one strand is built toward the fork and the other is built away from it. questions.question_text: Suggest one possible explanation for why some DNA samples show higher band intensity at specific fragment sizes than others.

questions.explanation: In automated electrophoresis (like the TapeStation system shown in Figure a), DNA fragments are separated by size and detected using a fluorescent dye. The "intensity" of a band on the resulting pattern refers to how bright or tall the peak is at a specific fragment size. Using the DNA Concentration Approach , we know that the intensity of a band is directly proportional to the amount of DNA in that specific location. A brighter or more intense band indicates that there is a higher concentration (or greater total mass) of DNA fragments of that specific length within the sample. This happens because more DNA molecules in that band bind to more fluorescent dye. Why would one sample have more fragments of a certain size than another? A common reason is that the sample contains more copies of that specific DNA sequence. This could be due to the nature of the original source or, very commonly in lab techniques, because that specific fragment was amplified more during a process like PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction). questions.question_text: Suggest a reason why RNA polymerase activity drops significantly at the terminator region.

questions.explanation: Looking at Figure 1, we can see that the activity of RNA polymerase remains high through the promoter and gene body, but it suddenly falls when it hits the terminator region . To explain this drop, we need to look at the specific molecular signals occurring at the end of a gene. The DNA sequence in this area contains specific transcription termination signals . These are unique sequences of bases that act as a 'stop' sign for the enzyme. This process is a core part of gene expression, which you can review in Topic D1.2: Protein synthesis . When the RNA polymerase encounters these signals, it undergoes a change that causes it to detach from the DNA template . Since the enzyme is no longer physically attached to the DNA to move along it, the recorded 'activity' drops to zero on the graph. At the same time the enzyme detaches, it must release the transcript (the completed mRNA strand). This completes the transcription process, allowing the mRNA to move on to translation and the RNA polymerase to be recycled for another round of transcription elsewhere.

questions.question_text: Explain how mutations in DNA can lead to genetic diseases.

questions.explanation: To understand how a disease forms, we have to look at the "blueprint" first. DNA contains the specific sequence of nitrogenous bases that codes for every protein in your body. A mutation is a structural change to this DNA sequence. When the DNA sequence is altered, the first step in the chain of events is that the mRNA produced during transcription will now carry a different set of codons. This relates to Topic D1.2: Protein synthesis , which explains how genes are expressed. Next, the altered mRNA moves to the ribosome for translation . Because the codons on the mRNA have changed, the tRNA molecules will bring different amino acids to the growing polypeptide chain.
